metaDescription: Six submersible utility pumps compared on minimum suction depth, motor size, cord length, switch style and build, for flooded floors, pools and tubs.
expertTake: The Little Giant 5-ASP-LL is the utility pump to buy if you want a brand with a real service record and a low shutoff level, the FOTING 1/2 HP with a stainless base is the best value for pulling water down to a film, and the AQUASTRONG 1 HP is the high-volume option for big jobs. Skip all of these as a permanent sump pump, because utility pumps are built to be dropped in, run and pulled out.
introParagraphs: A utility pump is the tool you grab when water is somewhere it should not be: a flooded cellar floor, a window well, a drained hot tub, a pool cover or a stock tank. It is a drop-in submersible, usually thermoplastic or aluminum, that you plug in, point a hose at and pull out when the job is done.

What separates a good one from a bad one is not horsepower. It is how low the pump can pull the water, how it is switched, how long the cord is, and whether the body survives a season in a garage between jobs. This guide sorts the field by those ownership details.

products.name: Little Giant 5-ASP-LL 1/6 HP automatic low-level utility pump
products.description:
The 5-ASP-LL is a low-level automatic pump built around a piggyback diaphragm switch and a 1/6 HP permanently lubricated PSC motor in an epoxy-coated die-cast aluminum body. Aluminum sheds heat well for a utility pump, and the oil-free motor means there is no oil to leak into your pool or tub.

Its diaphragm switch is a sealed design with no float arm to snag, which suits tight spaces like window wells and the bottom of a stock tank. An 18 foot cord and a 1 inch FNPT discharge make it easy to place and plumb. At 1,500 GPH it moves less than the 1 HP imports in this guide, but it is a smaller, more refined machine from a company with decades of experience.

The tradeoff is flow and price: you pay more for less rated volume. Ownership is simple: rinse the screen, store the pump dry and upright, and check the diaphragm switch if the pump ever fails to start. It is a tool you will still own in ten years. If you need more volume, move up to the AQUASTRONG; if you need more reach, the 5-MSP's longer cord wins. The 5-ASP-LL is the one to buy when you want a single pump that handles a dozen small jobs a year without drama.
products.bestFor: Low-level draining of cellars, window wells and tubs with a trusted brand.
pros: Sealed diaphragm switch has no float arm to snag
Aluminum body sheds heat and resists corrosion
18 ft cord reaches across a cellar
cons: 1,500 GPH is modest next to 1 HP imports

products.name: Little Giant 5-MSP 1/6 HP manual utility pump with 25 ft cord
products.description:
The 5-MSP is the manual cousin of the 5-ASP-LL: the same 1/6 HP motor class and aluminum body, but with no switch at all. You plug it in and it runs, and you unplug it when the job is done. That simplicity is the point, since there is no float or diaphragm to fail, and it is rated for general water transfer and recirculation.

A shaded pole motor is a simple, rugged design with modest efficiency, which suits a pump that runs for minutes rather than months. A 25 foot cord and a 1 inch FNPT discharge give it good reach. Because it has no automatic shutoff, you must watch it: running a submersible dry for long burns the seals.

It costs a little less than the automatic model and suits anyone who is standing there anyway. Rinse it, hang it up, and it will outlast most thermoplastic pumps. A small tip: tie a length of rope to the handle so you can pull it from a deep tub or well without touching the cord.
products.bestFor: Supervised jobs such as draining a pool cover or tub where you stand nearby.
pros: No switch to fail or snag
25 ft cord is the longest in the group
Aluminum body resists heat and corrosion
cons: No automatic shutoff, so it needs watching
Running dry can damage the seals

products.name: FOTING 1/2 HP stainless base utility pump 2,450 GPH
products.description:
This pump's party trick is a stainless steel base that lets it pull water down to 0.04 inch, about the thickness of a coin. For a flooded basement floor, that is the difference between squeegeeing the last quarter inch and leaving a film that grows mildew. Its thermoplastic body is light and corrosion resistant, and the motor is rated for about 2,000 uses.

A 1/2 HP motor gives it twice the rating of the Superior 91250 at 1/4 HP and moves 2,450 GPH at zero lift, with a rated head of 25 feet. The grain size limit of 1/5 inch means it handles clean to slightly dirty water, not mud.

It is a good value for flood cleanup and pool cover draining. Rinse the screen after each use, keep the base free of grit and store it dry. Its 2,000-use motor claim is a manufacturer figure, so treat it as a durability hint, not a guarantee, and compare it with the aluminum Little Giants for long-term ownership.
products.bestFor: Flooded floors where you need to pull the last film of water.
pros: Stainless base for stability and wear
1/2 HP motor with 25 ft head rating
cons: Thermoplastic body is not for permanent installation
Limited to grains up to 1/5 inch
No long warranty in the data

products.name: AQUASTRONG 1 HP utility pump 4,500 GPH with adapters
products.description:
The AQUASTRONG is the biggest hose-fed pump here: a 1 HP motor rated for 4,500 GPH at zero lift, a bottom suction intake with a debris filter and a 1-1/4 inch NPT outlet with several adapters. For a large flooded room or a pool, it empties the space far faster than the 1/6 HP Little Giants.

The cost is that the figure is a zero-lift rating, so at a real rise of ten feet the flow drops substantially, and a 1 HP motor draws a lot at startup. Bottom suction drains low, which is useful for floods. Compared with the FOTING 1/2 HP, it moves almost twice the volume on paper.

Use it for big drain jobs and keep it away from permanent pit duty. A thermoplastic body and no stated warranty term mean it is a tool, not an installation. Pair it with a long layflat discharge hose, since the 1-1/4 inch outlet is happiest on a short, straight run with few kinks.
products.bestFor: Big flooded rooms, pools and ponds where speed matters.
pros: Includes several hose and pipe adapters

products.name: Superior Pump 91250 1/4 HP utility pump 1,800 GPH
products.description:
The 91250 is a plain 1/4 HP thermoplastic pump with a 10 foot cord and a 25 foot lift rating. A 1-1/4 inch NPT outlet carries more water than a 1 inch outlet, and a garden hose adapter makes it ready for basic jobs out of the box.

It moves up to 1,800 GPH, slightly more than the Little Giant 1/6 HP units, and its price is low. Thermoplastic does not shed heat like aluminum, so keep runs short.

It makes a good garage spare. Rinse it, hang it and replace it if it starts to hum without moving water. It also doubles as a small pond or aquarium drain, provided the water is clean.
products.bestFor: A garage spare for occasional draining.

products.name: Cleartide 1/3 HP utility pump 2,790 GPH with water sensor
products.description:
The Cleartide uses an electronic sensor rather than a float. In auto mode it starts at about 1-1/5 inches of water and stops at about 1/5 inch, and a manual mode lets you finish the job. A 1/3 HP copper-wound motor is claimed to run cooler and last longer.

A sensor avoids the classic float snag, but it is a newer design, and silt can coat the probes. It moves 2,790 GPH on paper, more than the Superior and less than the AQUASTRONG.

It is a versatile pick for flooded floors. Wipe the sensor probes after each use and store it dry. The manual mode is handy for the last pass over a flooded floor, once the sensor has shut the pump off.
products.bestFor: Flooded floors where an auto sensor is convenient.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The suction level decides whether you finish the job. The FOTING 1/2 HP pulls to 0.04 inch, the Cleartide stops at about 1/5 inch, and most pumps quit near an inch or more. A film of water left on a basement floor is a mildew risk. A good approach is to keep a small wet vacuum or a squeegee for the last film, since no submersible pump leaves a floor truly dry. If the floor is carpeted, pull the carpet and pad first, because water trapped in the pad will keep wicking back.

Manual pumps like the Little Giant 5-MSP have nothing to fail but need watching. Floats can snag, diaphragm switches like the 5-ASP-LL are sealed, and sensors like the Cleartide's have no moving parts. Pick the style that fits how you will supervise the job. A float that sticks in the up position will run the pump dry, which is the most common way a cheap utility pump dies. Lift the float by hand before each job to confirm it moves.

Aluminum on the Little Giants sheds heat better than the thermoplastic on the Superior and AQUASTRONG. A utility pump runs for minutes, so heat matters less than for a sump pump, but long pool jobs can cook a plastic pump. Never run a thermoplastic pump out of water for more than a few seconds, because the water around the motor is the only cooling it has.

Rated GPH is at zero lift. The AQUASTRONG's 4,500 GPH and the Superior's 1,800 GPH both fall with every foot of rise. Count your actual height and hose length before trusting a label. A 25 foot head rating means the pump can push water that high, but it does so at a trickle, so for a second-floor discharge expect a much lower volume than the label.

A 1-1/4 inch outlet, as on the Superior and AQUASTRONG, carries more than a 1 inch outlet. Check the adapters match your hose, since a mismatch means a trip to the hardware store mid-flood. A cheap hose adapter that leaks at the pump wastes a surprising amount of flow, so tighten fittings and use a clamp.

The 5-MSP's 25 foot cord reaches across a cellar, while the Superior has 10 feet. Use a rated outdoor extension cord for wet jobs, and store pumps dry, upright and rinsed. Check the cord for a three-prong grounded plug, and use a GFCI outlet or adapter near any standing water.

specDecoder.meaning: The lowest water depth the pump can pull down to before it runs dry. A lower number means a drier floor but often a smaller, slower intake.
specDecoder.watchFor: The FOTING 1/2 HP lists 0.04 inch; many others stop near an inch.

specDecoder.meaning: A plug-through switch that controls the pump from one outlet. It is convenient because the pump and its switch share one outlet.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 5-ASP-LL uses a diaphragm piggyback switch.

specDecoder.meaning: A simple, low-torque motor design with modest efficiency.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 5-MSP uses one, which suits short runs.

specDecoder.meaning: The height at which flow drops to zero, not a working head. Real flow at a working head is always lower.
specDecoder.watchFor: The FOTING lists 25 feet; real flow is much lower near that.

specDecoder.meaning: The largest particle the intake screen passes. Larger grains will jam the impeller.
specDecoder.watchFor: The FOTING lists 1/5 inch, so mud will clog it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Shutoff depth
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared how low each pump can pull water. The FOTING at 0.04 inch and the Cleartide at about 1/5 inch lead. We also noted whether the minimum depth is stated or implied, since many listings omit it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Switching
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed manual, diaphragm, float and sensor controls against the failure mode of each. A sealed diaphragm or sensor scored higher in tight spaces than a swinging float.

howWeEvaluated.title: Body and heat
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared aluminum bodies against thermoplastic for long jobs. The Little Giants have the edge. Because utility jobs are short, we treated heat as a secondary issue for casual use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Real flow
howWeEvaluated.description: We read ratings as zero-lift ceilings. The AQUASTRONG's 4,500 GPH and the Little Giant's 1,500 GPH differ by a factor of three on paper. We cross-checked flow labels against horsepower to spot inflated numbers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at cord length, adapters and storage, and favored brands with a service record. Brand support counted for more than a small price difference.

rows: More motor and a low suction

cards.label: Aluminum
cards.text: The Little Giants shed heat and last for years, but move less water.

cards.label: Thermoplastic
cards.text: The Superior, FOTING and AQUASTRONG are light and cheap, and move more water, but are built for occasional use.

howToChoose.note: Aluminum for years of use, thermoplastic for a one-off job.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A low shutoff depth and a long cord. A film of water left behind grows mildew.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The FOTING 1/2 HP pulls to 0.04 inch and the Little Giant 5-MSP has 25 feet of cord.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You will use it for years. The Little Giant 5-ASP-LL has an aluminum body and a sealed switch.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: It is a one-time job. The Superior 91250 does the work.

maintenance.why: Silt dries and clogs the intake. Rinse it clean before storage. Flush with clean water if the job involved silt or pool chemicals.
Moisture in the motor corrodes the seals. Hang the pump by its handle. A pump stored on its side can collect water in the motor.
A damaged cord near water is a shock risk.
Silt on a sensor causes false readings. Wipe the Cleartide's probes.
A seized impeller burns the motor. Turn it by hand before the next job. It also catches the occasional bearing that has begun to bind.

faq.q: What is the difference between a utility pump and a sump pump?
faq.a: A utility pump is a portable drop-in for temporary draining. A sump pump is built for permanent pit duty with a durable switch and cooling. If you plan to leave a pump in a pit all year, buy a pit pump.

faq.q: Can I leave a utility pump running unattended?
faq.a: Only an automatic model with a float, diaphragm or sensor. Manual pumps burn their seals if they run dry. Check the float before every job, since a stuck float is the usual failure.

faq.q: How low can a utility pump drain?
faq.a: It depends on the intake design. The FOTING lists 0.04 inch while many pumps stop near an inch.

faq.q: Is a 1 HP utility pump better than a 1/4 HP?
faq.a: It moves more on paper but draws more current, and real flow falls at lift. Match the pump to the job. A bigger pump also needs a bigger discharge hose.

faq.q: Can a utility pump handle dirty water?
faq.a: Light debris, yes. Mud and gravel will clog the screen and wear the impeller. Use a pump with a stainless or aluminum body for gritty water.

faq.q: How do I store a utility pump?
faq.a: Rinse it, dry it, and hang it upright. Keep the cord loosely coiled. Never hang a pump by its cord.
